title: Why the UK left UNIDO and what to test before rejoining
label: 12 October 2026 · UNIDO evidence session
summary: Sir Andrew Mitchell, who led the UK decision to withdraw from the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) in 2010–12, explains why the UK left (limited poverty impact, weak country presence, poor financial management and transparency) and how UNIDO has changed since. He admits some reforms are real—more focus on green industry, improved oversight and project work—but says gaps remain in results measurement and accountability. He urges a cautious approach to rejoining, recommends rigorous independent evaluation using the original multilateral aid review criteria, and wants 2029 review commitments and parliamentary scrutiny.

speakers.label: Sir Andrew Mitchell
speakers.name: Sir Andrew Mitchell
speakers.role: Former Secretary of State for International Development

glossary.definition: United Nations Industrial Development Organization, a UN agency that promotes industrial development in poorer countries.
A UK government assessment (2010) that ranked UN and similar agencies on value for money and development impact.
Official Development Assistance — the UK government budget for overseas aid.
Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, a UK department that now funds some international climate and industrial programmes.
United Nations Development Programme — a UN agency that supports national development and poverty reduction.
United Nations Children's Fund, a UN agency focused on children's welfare.
International Organization for Migration, a UN-related agency dealing with migration issues.

chapters.title: Why the UK left UNIDO (2010–12)
chapters.takeaway: The UK withdrew because a formal review judged UNIDO had poor impact on poverty, weak country presence, and weak financial transparency.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Sir Andrew, thank you for joining us. You led the decision to leave UNIDO in 2010. Could you explain why the UK withdrew and whether you now regret it?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: When we formed government in 2010 we set a high bar for development spending. Parliament backed 0.7% of GNI for aid, so taxpayers needed to see clear results.

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: We created the multilateral aid review to test 43 UN agencies against UK interests and value for money. The public and experts could see the findings.

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: UNIDO fell into the group we could no longer justify funding. Key problems were: little evidence of impact on global poverty, a weak country-level presence, and poor financial management and transparency.

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: We withdrew membership over two years and saved roughly £7 million a year in membership fees. That didn’t stop funding specific projects where needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the decision was public and tested by experts. You say project funding could still continue even after leaving?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Yes. We stopped core membership payments but could (and did) pay for targeted projects when there was a clear UK interest or urgent need.

chapters.title: Have reforms made UNIDO acceptable now?
chapters.takeaway: There have been real reforms—more focus on green industry, better transparency and project work—but serious gaps in results measurement and accountability remain.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: UNIDO now has a new director-general and a different focus. Has it genuinely reformed enough to justify the UK rejoining?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: There are three important changes since my time. First, UNIDO now emphasises industrial decarbonisation and green supply chains — that’s closer to current UK priorities.

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Second, oversight and transparency have improved: it has an independent evaluation unit and claims to be leaner and more open than before.

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Third, the UK has shifted to funding specific UNIDO programmes — for example clean technology projects — rather than core membership in recent years.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So some reforms are real. Are there still management problems?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Yes. UNIDO’s own 2018–25 review found results management wasn’t fully implemented, data systems are fragmented, baselines incomplete, and accountability below senior levels is weak.

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: A nicer strategy and better units don’t prove that taxpayers’ money is delivering outcomes. That’s the crux of the remaining concern.

chapters.title: Money, membership and practical projects
chapters.takeaway: Membership fees were small but membership gives governance influence; large project funding is handled by other UK departments, and claimed leverage must be checked.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You mentioned saving £7 million a year. Is that the membership fee we stopped paying?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Yes — roughly £7 million annually was the cost of board membership that we cut when we withdrew.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But the UK has since channelled much larger sums through UNIDO for projects — we heard figures like £125m rising toward £200m. How does that fit?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: I don’t have exact numbers to hand. That programme-level money is not from the Foreign Office’s budget; much of it comes via DESNZ and specific climate or investment programmes.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: Is the UK better off running targeted bilateral projects ourselves, or funding UNIDO programmes?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Both approaches have merits. Bilateral work gives direct oversight — boots on the ground — but UNIDO can sometimes unlock larger finance if projects are well run. Each case must be judged for value and risk.

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: For example, a UK-funded UNIDO Brazil project used £15m of UK money to supposedly unlock £250m of development finance and projected private investment, though those leverage claims need verification.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: So the leverage is promising but not yet proven?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Exactly. That’s why independent evaluation matters before scaling up or tying membership to large spending commitments.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: Being on UNIDO’s governing board gives the UK a voice in decisions. But if we are a minority we could be tied to collective choices we don't like. Is that a concern?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Yes. Board membership partly implicates you in decisions. ‘Seat at the table’ arguments are attractive but must be tested against whether the influence gained justifies the cost and risks.

chapters.title: Checks, reviews and parliamentary scrutiny
chapters.takeaway: Rejoining should be coupled to clear, independent evaluation, use MAR-type criteria, a firm 2029 review date, and parliamentary oversight to hold government to account.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: Should the rejoining decision be formally reviewed later, and should Parliament be involved to strengthen our negotiating position?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Yes. The Government has proposed a 2029 review. That must be more than a gesture — it should be independent, use clear criteria and be available for parliamentary committees to scrutinise.

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Parliamentary scrutiny is an asset. It gives negotiators leverage to demand credible reporting and evidence of results from UNIDO.

turns.speaker: Lord Stevenson of Balmacara
turns.text: If we use the original MAR as a model, is that still appropriate given how UK capacity has changed since 2010?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: The MAR’s core questions remain useful: does the agency deliver development impact, value for money, additionality, good governance and sustainability? But the review must recognise current limits in UK bilateral capacity and draw on external experts.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: Who should do the review and how do we avoid a rubber-stamp exercise?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Commission independent experts, including academics and practitioners. Officials will be involved, but external evaluators should lead terms of reference and assessments, and Parliament should get the findings.

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: If UNIDO fails to meet standards on results and transparency, the UK must be prepared to reconsider membership — that’s what the MAR taught us.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Your position is cautious: UNIDO has improved but not fully met MAR concerns; rejoining must be justified by verified results, a 2029 review and parliamentary scrutiny.

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: Yes. Given a constrained ODA budget and the need to prioritise humanitarian and high-impact work, any decision to spend more through UNIDO must be robustly justified and reviewed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That is very helpful. No final points?

turns.speaker: Sir Andrew Mitchell
turns.text: No — just that your committee should press for a strong, independent 2029 review and insist on transparent reporting against MAR-style criteria.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Sir Andrew — we are grateful for your time and the clarity of your advice.
